message.content:
Let  
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41.
\]
Then
\[
p(n+1)=(n+1)^2-(n+1)+41=n^2+n+41.
\]

Any common factor of \(p(n)\) and \(p(n+1)\) must divide their difference:
\[
p(n+1)-p(n)=2n.
\]
So if \(d=\gcd(p(n),p(n+1))\), then \(d\mid 2n\).

Now note that
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41=n(n-1)+41.
\]
Thus
\[
\gcd(p(n),n)=\gcd(41,n).
\]
Also \(p(n)=n(n-1)+41\) is always odd because \(n(n-1)\) is even and \(41\) is odd. Therefore any common factor greater than \(1\) must be an odd divisor of \(n\), so it must divide \(41\).

Since \(41\) is prime, the only possible common factor greater than \(1\) is \(41\). This happens when \(n\) is a multiple of \(41\). The smallest positive such \(n\) is
\[
n=41.
\]

Check:
\[
p(41)=41^2-41+41=41^2,
\]
and
\[
p(42)=42^2-42+41=1763=41\cdot 43.
\]
So they share the factor \(41\).

The answer is 41.
